seat.BEST_WHY: The wall run along the top of the lit room, roughly (430–750, 395–450). The blocks vary in width course-to-course and the vertical joints don't stack — the joint at x≈600 in the upper course has no partner below it — and the joints vary in depth along a single run: some read as a near-black slot, others as a two-value step. That reads as cut and laid stone, not a stamped brick pattern. Driven into that run are thin dark vertical pins at x≈693 and x≈703 and a horizontal salvaged timber at (600–660, 400), placed at irregular intervals and not centred on any block — repairs made by someone solving a problem, not decorating. Second thing that's genuinely well made: the floor around the figure holds its structure under the light. Sampling y=545 across x=300–470, the joints still step (204, 204, 204, 200) inside the brightest area, so the grid survives the highlight and the floor keeps its scale where the eye actually goes.
seat.WORST_WHY: The flagstone floor is a flat fill with a grid drawn on top. The band at (40–340, 230–258) contains 7 unique colours total, and one of them — a neutral #5A5A5A — covers 87% of the pixels. Every channel is equal: mean saturation across that band is 0.54/255. The stone has no material colour, no bedding, no wear, no variation between one slab and the next; the only thing distinguishing two adjacent flagstones is the 1px joint line between them. Second: the water at roughly (248–345, 0–192) is an axis-aligned rectangle. Its left edge is a dead-straight vertical cut against the dirt, its bottom edge a dead-straight horizontal one, with no bank, no shoreline tile, no darkening at depth, no wetting of the dirt it touches. It is a green rectangle placed on a brown rectangle. Third: the two barrels at (118,190) and (160,190) and the two crates at (65,0)–(95,75) are drawn in side elevation — visible staves, elliptical lids, a crate front face with a latch — sitting in an otherwise strictly top-down field, and none of the four casts a contact shadow.
seat.FLAGGED:
1, 2, 3

For 1: the clipping. Along y=545, x≈365–425 the floor runs 244, 244, 244, 243 — a flat plateau with the joints erased, in the exact centre of the frame. Then the diagonal hatch streaks through (300–430, 470–600) at about 30°, crossing tile boundaries and appearing nowhere else in the image. It reads as a bloom pass run over the tiles.

For 3 (and 1, same sprite): the figure holds a sword in one hand and a round bullseye shield in the other. It is carrying no light. The frame's entire light model originates at its feet from nothing. That is the first thing a person looks at and there is no lamp there.

For 2: the water rectangle, and the elevation-view props in a top-down field.

flip_list: The figure at (385–430, 460–510) carries sword and shield and no light source, while the only light in the frame originates at its feet. Put a hooded lamp in the shield hand or hung at the belt, and move the light origin to the lamp.

That sprite is the only object in the frame with an outline — a black inner line plus a cream outer line, visible all around the helmet and boots — and the only one using saturated cyan (~#8FD8D8) and pure orange. Nothing in the environment uses an outline or either hue. Repaint it onto the environment's tan/umber/soot ramp and drop to a single dark outline or none.

At (450–530, 380–470) the wall's top surface and the lit corridor floor both sit at L≈190–210 and carry the same speckle; only a 1–2px dark line separates them. Drop the wall top ~25 values and give it a coarser, larger-scale grain than the floor.

The wall tops at (390–490, 70–190) and (620–750, 70–190) have no joints at all — they are soft airbrushed cloud. Draw the same block courses used at (430–750, 400–450) and let value, not blur, take them into the dark.

The object at (275–380, 640–710) reads as nothing: soft rim on all four sides, an interior of four arbitrary lighter and darker rectangles, no top plane, no side plane, and its left edge lands mid-tile. Resolve it into a named object — hatch, crate, grating — with a hard top edge and one visible side face, or delete it.
The crack descending from (330, 600) stops dead at that object's top-left corner and a different crack restarts at its right edge. Run one continuous crack under it, or terminate it into something.

23.4% of the frame sits below L=8 — flat void carrying no information. Raise the ambient floor to L≈14–18 so the unlit rooms at (0–180, 150–640) and (620–750, 150–300) still show block courses in silhouette.

The place is described as held by orc-soldiers repairing with rope, pins, hide and salvaged timber. One timber and two pins appear, all in the same wall run at (600–710, 400). Nothing in the other 90% of the frame has been touched by anyone. Carry the repair vocabulary into the floor and the far walls.

_build_id_restamped.why: SECOND RE-STAMP, 2026-09-07: the exclusion prefix-match fix pulled REVIEW_BUILD.json.template — a shipped input it had been hiding — into the hash. Again the FUNCTION changed, not the build. The build_id FUNCTION changed by ruling, not the build. RULED (Rafe, 2026-09-07): 'narrow build_id to the build. The id hashes shipped inputs only — game source, assets, shaders, scene/theme configs, output-affecting build scripts — and excludes the review layer's source, .claude/skills, and docs/ on the stated ground: they describe the build, they are not in it.' Bible §13.11's third instance. The old id was computed by the broad function and is not comparable with the new one, so it is recomputed rather than left to fail a comparison between two different functions.
_build_id_restamped.the_guarantee_that_did_not_move: THE DELIVERED FRAME. build_frame.sha256 is 8745c556dd1bef10 before and after — the same bytes the seat judged. That, not the id, is what the verdict is a claim about; the id is a cheap proxy for it, and re-stamping is only lawful BECAUSE the frame is identical. This script asserts that and refuses if it is not.
